what: Two cases per gate, one just inside its threshold and one just outside, so every gate on both lists has a pass and a fail from a case built to be exactly that.
whatItCannotSay: Nothing about the market. These are constructed numbers, and they encode this author's reading of each gate, which is why the expectation over them is produced by a second implementation in tools/derive-indicators.py --gates rather than by the rules themselves. Branch coverage is the only question they answer; the captured fixture answers whether the arithmetic still does what it did on a real day.
whyNotAWiderFixture: Measured at 2.6: eight of the ten long gates were one-sided over the captured fixture. Thirty names on one session record two setups, so a gate with two results is one-sided unless those two disagree. The remedy priced at 2.6 was a second as-of date at 33 per-ticker calls; it would have left those eight gates with three results each. A bigger instance of the wrong instrument.
knownLimitation: A gate with several clauses has one of them at its boundary, named in the case's why line, and the others tested only by the all-passing baseline. tradable and tradable-shortable are the two: the first sits on its liquidity floor, the second on its listing-age floor, which is the floor unique to it. The all-absent proof covers every clause of every gate for absence, and not for a boundary.
